title: Present Perfect Continuous
tagline: how long, and why: have / has been + -ing
why: We use the present perfect continuous to say how long an activity has been going on, and to explain what we can see now: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?
know: for + a length of time, since + a starting point, and the question How long...?
state verbs that stay in the present perfect simple: know, have (own), be, want
understand: the difference between the activity (I've been painting) and the result (I've painted two rooms)
why we say I've known her for years, not I've been knowing her
able: say how long you have been doing something: I've been learning English for two years.
explain a result you can see: I'm hot because I've been running.
mistakes: I am learning English for three years.
I have been learning English for three years.
I have been knowing him since school.
She has been work here since May.
She has been working here since May.
How long you have been waiting?
I've been reading three books this month.
I've read three books this month.
use: how long an activity has continued up to now: We've been waiting for forty minutes.
a recent activity with a result you can see: The ground is wet. It's been raining.
repeated actions up to now: He's been calling me all morning.
form: I haven't been sleeping well. He hasn't been working long.
Have you been waiting long? How long has she been living here?
signals: for (two hours, ages, a long time), since (9 o'clock, Monday, 2019), How long...?, all day, all morning, lately, recently
tip: Activity or result? Use the continuous for the activity and how long: I've been cooking all afternoon. Use the simple for the result or how many: I've cooked three dishes. State verbs always use the simple: I've had this car for years.

pick.q: I ___ since 7 a.m. and I need a break.
pick.why: Since 7 a.m. until now: have been working. Don't use the present with since.

pick.q: We ___ for the bus for twenty minutes.
pick.why: For twenty minutes until now: have been waiting.

pick.q: I ___ my neighbour for ten years.
pick.why: Know is a state verb, so use the present perfect simple: I have known.
A result you can see: What have you been doing? Use been + -ing, with have before you.
How many = the result, so use the simple: She has made three cakes.

pick.q: It ___ since Tuesday. The streets are flooded.
pick.why: Since Tuesday until now, with a result you can see: has been raining.
How long + until now: How long have you been learning Spanish?
Have meaning own is a state verb, so use the simple: He has had that truck since 2005.

type.q: She ___ (study) for her exam since eight o'clock this morning.
type.why: Since eight o'clock until now: has been studying.

type.q: How long ___ (you / wait) for the doctor?
type.why: How long + until now: How long have you been waiting?

type.q: They ___ (not / sleep) well since the baby was born.
type.why: Since the baby was born until now: haven't been sleeping (or haven't slept) well.

type.q: I ___ (know) Ahmed since we were at school together.
type.why: Know is a state verb, so no -ing: I have known Ahmed.

type.q: It ___ (snow) for three hours. The roads are terrible.
type.why: For three hours until now, with a result: has been snowing.

type.q: He ___ (drive) for six hours, so he needs a rest.
type.why: An activity until now with a result (he's tired): has been driving.

type.q: We ___ (paint) the living room all weekend. Look at our clothes!
type.why: A long activity with a result you can see: have been painting.

type.q: My phone ___ (ring) all morning. Everyone wants something.
type.why: A repeated action until now: has been ringing.

spot.q: I am waiting here since ten o'clock.
spot.why: Since ten o'clock until now: I have been waiting here since ten o'clock.

spot.q: She has been knowing about the problem for weeks.
spot.why: Know is a state verb, so no -ing: She has known about the problem for weeks.

spot.q: We have been live in Toronto for five years.
spot.why: After been, use the -ing form: We have been living in Toronto for five years.

spot.q: How long are you working at the bank?
spot.why: How long until now needs the present perfect: How long have you been working at the bank?

spot.q: I have been drinking four cups of coffee today.
spot.why: How many = the result, so use the simple: I have drunk four cups of coffee today.

order.a: How long have you been learning English?
It has been raining since early this morning.
alt: Since early this morning it has been raining.
order.why: Has been + -ing, with since + a starting point.

order.a: She has been working from home since March.
alt: Since March she has been working from home.
order.why: Has been + -ing for an activity from March until now.

order.a: They have been looking for a new apartment.
order.why: Have been + -ing for an activity that is still going on.

pick.why: A result you can notice: Have you been cooking? Been goes with have.

pick.q: He ___ at the computer for five hours. His eyes hurt.
pick.why: For five hours until now: has been sitting.

pick.q: I ___ this jacket for twenty years!
pick.why: Have meaning own is a state verb, so use the simple: I have had this jacket.
2012 is a starting point, so use since.

pick.q: We have been talking ___ an hour.
pick.why: An hour is a length of time, so use for.

pick.q: I ___ two chapters of my book today.
pick.why: How many = the result, so use the simple: I have read two chapters.

type.q: My son ___ (play) video games since lunch!
type.why: Since lunch until now: has been playing.
Lately = up to now: I haven't been feeling well (or haven't felt well).
How long + until now: has she been living (or has she lived)?

type.q: We ___ (try) to call you all day. Where were you?
type.why: A repeated activity all day until now: have been trying.

type.q: He ___ (be) my doctor for ten years.
type.why: Be is a state verb, so use the simple: He has been my doctor for ten years.
A result you can see: Have you been running?

type.q: The neighbours ___ (argue) for hours. I can hear them through the wall.
type.why: For hours until now: have been arguing.

type.q: I ___ (wait) for this parcel for two weeks.
type.why: For two weeks until now: have been waiting.

spot.q: I have been loving this city since my first visit.
spot.why: Love is a state verb, so use the simple: I have loved this city since my first visit.

spot.q: He has been fix the car all morning.
spot.why: After been, use the -ing form: He has been fixing the car all morning.

spot.q: We are knowing each other since university.
spot.why: Know is a state verb, and since needs the present perfect: We have known each other.

spot.q: She has been working here since two years.
spot.why: Two years is a length of time, so use for: She has been working here for two years.

order.a: What have you been doing all day?
My brother has been travelling around Europe since June.
alt: Since June my brother has been travelling around Europe.
order.why: Has been + -ing for an activity from June until now.

order.a: We haven't been sleeping well this week.
alt: This week we haven't been sleeping well.
order.why: Haven't + been + -ing: We haven't been sleeping well.

bank.q: I ___ for a new job since January.
bank.why: Since January until now: have been looking.
A result you can see now: It has been raining.

bank.q: She ___ that bag since she was a student.
bank.why: Have meaning own is a state verb, so use the simple: She has had that bag.
How long until now: How long have you been working? Have comes before you.

bank.q: We have been driving ___ five hours.
bank.why: Five hours is a length of time, so use for.

bank.q: He ___ three emails to the landlord, but he hasn't had an answer.
bank.why: How many = the result, so use the simple: He has written three emails.

bank.q: They ___ about the trip since breakfast.
bank.why: Since breakfast until now: have been talking.
After been, use -ing. Sit doubles the t: sitting.

bank.q: My husband ___ (fix) the sink for two hours, and it still leaks.
bank.why: For two hours until now, still not finished: has been fixing.
How long until now: have you been studying (or have you studied)?

bank.q: I ___ (want) to visit Japan since I was a child.
bank.why: Want is a state verb, so no -ing: I have wanted to visit Japan.

bank.q: The kids are dirty. They ___ (play) in the mud.
bank.why: A result you can see: They have been playing in the mud.

bank.q: She ___ (not / work) here for very long.
bank.why: For until now: She hasn't been working (or hasn't worked) here for long.

bank.q: I am living in this house since 1998.
bank.why: Since 1998 until now needs the present perfect: I have been living in this house.

bank.q: He has been owning this restaurant for ten years.
bank.why: Own is a state verb, so no -ing: He has owned this restaurant for ten years.

bank.q: We've been waiting for the plumber since eight o'clock.
bank.why: Correct! Since eight o'clock until now: we've been waiting.

bank.q: I've had a headache since lunch.
bank.why: Correct! Have a headache is a state, so we use the simple: I've had.

bank.a: Have you been waiting for a long time?
bank.why: Have + you + been + -ing: Have you been waiting for a long time?

bank.a: He has been coughing all night.
bank.why: Has been + -ing for a repeated action until now.

bank.a: I haven't been going to the gym lately.
alt: Lately I haven't been going to the gym.
bank.why: Haven't + been + -ing. Lately can go at the end or the start.
